facts.text: Radar sends radio waves and measures object distance from their echoes and approach or recession speed from a shift in the returned frequency.
facts.quote: A radar sends out radio waves and listens for their echoes, measuring both the distance to objects and, from a shift in the returned frequency, how fast they approach or recede.

facts.text: Vehicle radars operate in the 77 GHz band, with radio wavelengths of about 4 millimeters.
facts.quote: Vehicle radars work in the 77 gigahertz (GHz) band, radio waves about 4 millimeters long.

facts.text: Radar measures closing speed directly through the Doppler effect, without waiting for several frames.
facts.quote: so closing speed is measured directly, without waiting for several frames.

facts.text: Radar cross-section (RCS) measures how large an object appears to radar in square meters; a metal plate has a huge RCS and a person a small RCS, so a dummy with correct camera appearance may have incorrect RCS.
facts.quote: Radar cross-section (RCS) is how big an object looks to the radar, in square meters; a metal plate has a huge RCS and a person a small one, so a dummy with the right camera appearance may have the wrong RCS [Chapter 3].

facts.text: Radar multipath creates ghost objects at incorrect positions when a wave bounces off two or more surfaces before returning.
facts.quote: Multipath is a wave bouncing off two or more surfaces before returning, which creates ghost objects at wrong positions.

facts.text: Radar clutter consists of unwanted echoes from ground, rain, the machine's own body and nearby structures.
facts.quote: Clutter is the mass of unwanted echoes from ground, rain, the machine's own body and nearby structures.

facts.text: Radar MIMO (multiple input, multiple output) uses several transmitting and receiving antennas together to measure angle more finely.
facts.quote: MIMO (multiple input, multiple output) means several transmitting and receiving antennas working together to measure angle more finely.

facts.text: Radar CFAR (constant false alarm rate) sets detection thresholds relative to local clutter so noise produces false detections at a fixed, low rate.
facts.quote: CFAR (constant false alarm rate) is the detection rule that sets the threshold relative to the local clutter so that noise produces false detections at a fixed, low rate.

facts.text: Radar is largely unaffected by airborne dust, mildly affected by fog and unaffected by darkness.
facts.quote: Radar is largely unaffected by airborne dust, only mildly by fog, and not at all by darkness [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Radar perceives shapes coarsely and is confused by metal and water.
facts.quote: But it sees shapes coarsely and is confused by metal and water.

facts.text: In the booklet's most relevant heavy-machine radar experiment, a radar mounted on a wheel loader in a hall encountered highly reflective thin metal pillars.
facts.quote: The most relevant heavy-machine experiment put a radar on a wheel loader in a hall: thin metal pillars were highly reflective

facts.text: The wheel-loader hall radar simulation matched measurements only after hand-built geometry and material tuning, and still omitted some real double reflections.
facts.quote: the simulation matched only after hand-built geometry and tuned materials, some real double reflections were still missing

facts.text: In the wheel-loader hall experiment, a detector trained on real radar data failed on most simulated images.
facts.quote: a detector trained on real radar data failed on most simulated images [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Material properties at 77 GHz often must be estimated from measurements.
facts.quote: Material properties at 77 GHz often have to be estimated from measurements

facts.text: Heavy rain produces radar clutter detections at very short range, where slow braking occurs.
facts.quote: heavy rain produces clutter detections at very short range, exactly where slow braking happens [Chapter 6].

facts.text: A 2006 study of radar on a 260-ton haul truck recorded 580 alarms over 618 reversals: 102 false alarms (18%), 243 nuisance alarms (42%) and 235 alarms requiring action (41%).
facts.quote: In a 2006 study of a radar system on a 260-ton haul truck, 580 alarms over 618 reversals split into 102 false (18%), 243 nuisance (42%) and 235 (41%) requiring action

facts.text: The haul truck's rear tires and protruding structures triggered false radar alarms in the 2006 study.
facts.quote: the truck's own rear tires and protruding structures triggered false alarms [Chapters 4, 7].

facts.text: A single rear radar missed people near the rear tires; two antennas about 1.8 meters apart with inward-crossed beams improved detection.
facts.quote: A single rear radar missed people near the rear tires; two antennas about 1.8 m apart with beams crossed inward improved detection [Chapter 9].

facts.text: Radar is the most mature sensor case for bench testing using a target emulator that returns artificial echoes to the real sensor.
facts.quote: Radar is also the most mature case for bench testing with a target emulator that returns artificial echoes to the real sensor [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Radar is the sensor most likely to keep working in dust and at night, but the booklet considers radar simulation of off-road clutter such as spoil piles, tires and rock faces low credibility until validated against the company's own measurements.
facts.quote: Radar is the sensor most likely to keep working in dust and at night, but the booklet treats radar simulation of off-road clutter (spoil piles, tires, rock faces) as low credibility until validated against the company's own measurements [Chapter 9].
